sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: mile-post numbers, work-zone devices and fines, and yellow versus white line rules
Look-alike numbers, devices and line patterns from the guide-sign, work-zone and pavement-marking pages, each tied to one handbook page; hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec12-R01 | anchor: A01
A mile post sits 2 feet off the right shoulder, and the posts are spaced about 1 mile apart, so one number is an offset and the other is a spacing. [A01]
Why it matters: group mile posts; difficulty two; confusable sec12-F06 versus sec12-F07.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec12-R02 | anchor: A01
A long-term work zone uses permanent signs, while a temporary work area uses portable signs that may stay up for only a few hours. [A01]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty two; prereq sec12-F10.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec12-R03 | anchor: A01
Buses and gasoline tankers must stop at railroad crossings, so be ready for the vehicle ahead of you to stop there. [A01]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty one; prereq sec12-F02.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec12-R04 | anchor: A02
The doubled fine described for work zones applies to a speed violation when the work-zone signs are posted. [A02]
Why it matters: group work-zone fines; difficulty two; prereq sec12-F18.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec12-R05 | anchor: A02
A flagger is a person in orange who stops, slows or guides traffic, while a flashing arrow panel is a lighted board that tells you to merge. [A02]
Why it matters: group work-zone devices; difficulty two; confusable sec12-F20 versus sec12-F24.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec12-R06 | anchor: A02
A flashing arrow panel asks you to change lanes in the arrow's direction, while an electronic message sign gives advance information such as closures, special directions or weather. [A02]
Why it matters: group work-zone devices; difficulty two; confusable sec12-F23 versus sec12-F25.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec12-R07 | anchor: A02
Construction and maintenance signs warn of danger near the work area, while cones, drums and barricades guide you through the work area itself. [A02]
Why it matters: group work-zone devices; difficulty two; confusable sec12-F21 versus sec12-F26.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec12-R08 | anchor: A03
Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, while white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction. [A03]
Why it matters: group line colors; difficulty one; confusable sec12-F29 versus sec12-F30.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec12-R09 | anchor: A03
With a broken yellow line on your side you may pass when the road is clear, but with a solid yellow line on your side you may not pass. [A03]
Why it matters: group yellow lines; difficulty three; confusable sec12-F33 versus sec12-F34.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec12-R10 | anchor: A03
Double solid yellow lines may be crossed only to turn left, while broken white lines may be crossed with caution to change lanes after signaling. [A03]
Why it matters: group crossing lines; difficulty three; confusable sec12-F35 versus sec12-F36.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec12-R11 | anchor: A03
Broken white lines may be crossed with caution, while solid white lines mark turn lanes and keep drivers from changing lanes near intersections. [A03]
Why it matters: group white lines; difficulty two; confusable sec12-F36 versus sec12-F37.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec12-R12 | anchor: A03
A curved arrow with the word ONLY requires the turn, while a lane with a curved arrow and a straight arrow lets you turn or continue straight. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane arrows; difficulty two; confusable sec12-F38 versus sec12-F39.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0045]
